question.value: What is the detailed structure of the dust ring and central cavity in the Oph IRS 48 transition disk, and what are the implications for its inner disk, orbital eccentricity, and proper motion of the crescent-shaped structure?

evidence.quote: In this work, we present deep dust continuum observation with high resolution towards the Oph IRS 48 system. For the first time, we are able to significantly trace and detect emission along $95\%$ of the ring crossing the crescent-shaped structure.
We also discuss the implications of the potential eccentric orbit on the proper motion of the crescent, the putative secondary companion, and the asymmetry in velocity maps.
A detection of the inner disk in the IRS 48 system will confirm its classification as a PTD, and help us understand the evolution of transition disks.

claims.hypothesis: The faint dust emission outside the main crescent in IRS 48 traces an eccentric ring rather than a circular ring.
claims.experiment: Deproject the deep high-resolution Band 7 continuum image using i = 50 deg and PA = 100 deg, and fit an ellipse with one focus at the central star by minimizing an intensity-weighted radial distance loss function.
claims.result: Emission is detected along 95% of the ring, which is best fit by an ellipse with semi-major axis a = 0.57'' (78 au), eccentricity e = 0.27, and aphelion-to-perihelion ratio 1.78.
claims.finding: The dust ring crossing the crescent in IRS 48 is highly eccentric with an eccentricity of 0.27.

evidence.quote: For the first time, we are able to significantly trace and detect emission along $95\%$ of the ring crossing the crescent-shaped structure. The ring is highly eccentric with an eccentricity of $0.27$.
The best fit has a semi-major axis $a=0.57''$, or $78$ au, and an eccentricity $e=0.27$.

claims.hypothesis: The compact submillimeter emission detected toward the central star originates from an unresolved inner circumstellar dust disk inside the cavity rather than the stellar photosphere or an ionized wind.
claims.experiment: Fit a 2D Gaussian to the central 15-sigma source, compare its 343.5 GHz flux (221 uJy) with expected stellar blackbody emission and extrapolated 34 GHz optically thin free-free jet emission, and calculate the optically thin dust mass.
claims.result: The central source is unresolved (0.095'' x 0.052''), located 3 mas from the Gaia star position, and its flux exceeds the stellar photosphere (7.22 uJy) by 21x and optically thin free-free wind emission (29 uJy) by ~10x, yielding a dust mass of 1.5e-8 M_sun (0.005 M_earth).
claims.finding: Compact emission is detected toward the central star, consistent with an unresolved inner dust disk of radius at most a couple of au and dust mass 0.005 M_earth.

evidence.quote: Neither the emission from the protostellar photosphere, nor the emission from an ionized wind could alone (or added) explain the measured flux from the central source in the ALMA image.

The dust mass is estimated as about $1.5\times 10^{-8}\rm\, M_\odot$, or $0.005\rm\, M_\oplus$, if the emission is mm-sized dust thermal emission. We do not resolve the central emission with $0.1''$ beam. If the central object is an unresolved inner disk, the disk radius is a couple of astronomical units at most.

claims.hypothesis: The crescent-shaped dust structure moves along the fitted eccentric orbit at a super-Keplerian speed (~1.13 v_K) near perihelion.
claims.experiment: Fit 2D Gaussians with CASA imfit to the crescent peak across 5 ALMA epochs spanning 2012 to 2021, subtract the Gaia DR3 stellar proper motion, and compare the trajectory with circular and eccentric orbits.
claims.result: The star-subtracted proper motion is (-3.0 +/- 1.9, 3.0 +/- 2.5) mas/yr, corresponding to a magnitude of 0.49 +/- 0.26 v_K, and the multi-epoch positions do not follow either the circular or best-fit elliptical orbit.
claims.finding: Existing multi-epoch astrometric data do not support either a circular orbit or the fitted elliptical orbit for the proper motion of the crescent peak.

evidence.quote: The magnitude of the proper motion is $0.49\pm 0.26\, v_K$.
We can see that the data points do not follow either a circular orbit or an eccentric orbit.
We fit the proper motion of the crescent-shaped dust structure as $0.49\pm 0.26\, v_K$. Existing data do not support either circular orbit or elliptical orbit.

claims.hypothesis: An eccentric orbit (e = 0.27) where gas co-moves with dust can explain the observed asymmetry between red-shifted and blue-shifted regions in molecular line velocity maps of IRS 48.
claims.experiment: Calculate the line-of-sight velocity map and iso-velocity contours for the e = 0.27 elliptical orbit assuming v_sys = 4.55 km/s and compare with a circular Keplerian model and published H2CO and 13CO observations.
claims.result: The elliptical orbit model produces larger red-shifted iso-velocity contours than blue-shifted contours because the western part of the disk is closer to perihelion, matching the qualitative asymmetry seen in H2CO and 13CO maps.
claims.finding: The velocity map asymmetry qualitatively supports the elliptical orbit, though quantitative consistency with e = 0.27 remains to be determined.

evidence.quote: We can see that the red region is significantly larger than the blue region, and the red-shifted solid contours are larger than their blue-shifted counterparts.

This asymmetry that the red-shifted contours are larger than their blue-shifted counterparts in velocity maps is visible in both $\rm H_2CO$ and $\rm ^{13}CO$ (cite: vanderMarel2014; vanderMarel2021_IRS48), which lends support to the elliptical orbit (as first discussed by (cite: Calcino2019)), although it remains to be determined whether the velocity map is quantitatively consistent with the eccentricity of $e=0.27$ inferred from the dust emission distribution.

why_this_data.value: Deep, high-resolution Band 7 observations (originally designed for dust polarization) provide the sensitivity (14 uJy/beam) and resolution (0.11'' x 0.072'') needed to trace faint dust emission around the full ring and resolve the inner cavity emission from the outer crescent.

evidence.quote: The experiment was primarily designed for studying the polarization of the dust emission toward IRS 48. Hence, we tuned four ALMA basebands dedicated for the dust continuum emission

Our ALMA observations are the deepest high resolution (sub)mm observations towards IRS 48 to date, reaching a noise level of $14\rm\, \mu Jy/beam$ at an angular resolution of $0.11\ensuremath{''}\times 0.072\ensuremath{''}$. For the first time we are able to significantly trace and detect emission from about $95\%$ of the ring crossing the crescent-shaped structure.

why_this_method.value: An asymmetric radial loss function was engineered for the ellipse fit to force the fitted ellipse to pass through the central peak of the crescent-shaped structure.

evidence.quote: The loss function is engineered to have our fitted ellipse crossing the central peak of the crescent-shaped structure, as the one we present in the next paragraph.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Circular orbit for the dust ring — rejected because the northern part of the ring is ~1.8 times further from the central star than the southern crescent peak.

evidence.quote: We can see that the north-northwest tail behind the crescent-shaped structure and the diffuse emission in the northwest part of the disk structure form an elliptical pattern rather than a circular pattern.
The necessity for the ring to be eccentric is clear given that the north part is $\sim 1.8$ times further from the central star than the peak

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Protostellar photosphere emission as the origin of the central source — rejected because the expected 870 um photospheric flux is 7.22e-6 Jy, which is 21 times smaller than detected.

evidence.quote: Firstly, the central emission cannot be completely explained by emission coming from a central star.
We can then calculate the flux density at the wavelength of $870\rm\, \mu m$ as $7.22\times 10^{-6}\rm\, Jy$. This is $21$ times smaller than what we detect.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Optically thin thermal free-free emission from an ionized wind/jet as the origin of the central source — rejected because extrapolating the 34 GHz flux (36 uJy) with spectral index -0.1 gives 29 uJy at 343.5 GHz, roughly 10 times smaller than measured.

evidence.quote: Assuming that the emission of a thermal jet is optically thin from 34 to 343.5 GHz, the free-free contribution would be $29 \mu$Jy at 343.5 GHz, roughly 10 times smaller than the measured flux.
Neither the emission from the protostellar photosphere, nor the emission from an ionized wind could alone (or added) explain the measured flux from the central source in the ALMA image.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Non-thermal magnetospheric synchrotron emission, ionized emission from the dust sublimation wall, or pebble/planetesimal collisions — set aside in favor of the simpler thermal inner disk hypothesis.

evidence.quote: Still other possible contributions can be due to the non-thermal synchrotron emission from the protostellar magnetosphere (cite: Andre1997), the ionized emission from the dust sublimation wall (cite: 2020AnezLopez), or the collisions from pebbles and planetesimals that heat the dust of a disk (cite: 2020Matra). The former two hypotheses are expected to be more prominent in the centimeter wavelength range, while the third hypothesis is somehow a more exotic solution that may need more theoretical work to be supported.

limitations_admitted.value: The emission along ~5% of the ellipse is not robustly detected, so only a lower limit (>=400) can be placed on the maximum-to-minimum intensity ratio.

evidence.quote: Since the emission along part of the ellipse is not robustly detected, the ratio of the maximum intensity is at least 400 times the minimum.

limitations_admitted.value: The central source is not spatially resolved by the 0.1'' beam, so its radius is only constrained as an upper limit.

evidence.quote: We do not resolve the central emission with $0.1''$ beam. If the central object is an unresolved inner disk, the disk radius is a couple of astronomical units at most.

limitations_admitted.value: The proper motion analysis combines Band 9 (440 um) and Band 7 (870 um) observations and ignores Gaia astrometric errors and potential primary star reflex motion due to an unseen companion.

evidence.quote: We do not consider the astrometric error from Gaia.
We note that the first two points, from (cite: vanderMarel2013) and (cite: vanderMarel2015), are observed at Band 9 ($440\rm\, \mu m$), whereas the others are observed at Band 7 ($870\rm\, \mu m$).

in the case of an undetected stellar companion with a non-negligible mass (as suggested by (cite: Calcino2019)), the Gaia proper motions do not take into account the possible orbital motion of the primary star.

limitations_admitted.value: When the ellipse focus is allowed to vary freely, the dispersed nature of the dust emission leaves the focus location degenerate over ~50 au.

evidence.quote: Despite the similarity in their loss functions, the location of the foci differs by almost $50$ au.
The uncertainty of the fitted focus mostly comes from the dispersed nature of the emission. Deeper observations with lower noise are unlikely to give much better constraints.

limitations_admitted.value: Quantitative consistency between the gas velocity map and the e = 0.27 dust ring eccentricity has not yet been established.

evidence.quote: although it remains to be determined whether the velocity map is quantitatively consistent with the eccentricity of $e=0.27$ inferred from the dust emission distribution.

referee_caveats_inferred: Fitting a 2D Gaussian (via CASA imfit) to a strongly asymmetric, crescent-shaped structure across epochs with very different beam sizes (from 0.49''x0.39'' to 0.11''x0.072'') can introduce systematic resolution-dependent shifts in the fitted centroid compared to the true peak.

The custom loss function L = sum I(x,y) f(dr) weights pixels linearly by intensity I(x,y); because the crescent peak has an intensity contrast of ~270-400 relative to the faint northern ring, the fit is heavily dominated by the bright crescent unless an explicit mask or log-scaling is applied.

Phase-only self-calibration was performed on the 2021 data; although the authors checked that peak positions before and after self-calibration agreed, any initial phase-center offset prior to self-calibration directly enters the 2021 epoch astrometry.
